Adult brown-throated sloths typically attain an ultimate body mass of approximately 5000 grams [Wwi = approximately 5000 grams], a value that falls within the middle of the reported range for the species, which extends from 2.25 to 6.3 kilograms. Newborn pups emerge after a gestation period of about 213.5 days [tg = about 213.5 days] at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a duration that is prolonged relative to many other placental mammals of comparable adult size, reflecting the sloth's exceptionally low metabolic rate. At the moment of parturition, a neonate weighs a modest 179 grams [Wwb = 179 grams], a figure initially inferred from the closely related congener Bradypus tridactylus and since corroborated by field observations of Bradypus variegatus. This altricial neonate is entirely dependent on its mother for warmth and nutrition, and the immediate postnatal period is characterized by sustained nursing and close physical contact within the forest canopy. The relatively small birth mass is consistent with the species’ overall slow life-history strategy, which prioritizes low energetic expenditure over rapid offspring production.

Weaning marks a critical dietary transition for the growing juvenile, and the time since birth at weaning has been documented as approximately 31.5 days [tx = approximately 31.5 days] under the stable thermal conditions of the Neotropical lowland forests it inhabits at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. At this point, the pup has reached a weaning mass of 306 grams [Wwx = 306 grams], having nearly doubled its birth weight through a steady, though unhurried, period of maternal milk provisioning. The cessation of lactation coincides with the offspring’s first independent forays into the canopy to feed on young leaves, though the mother continues to provide close protection for several more weeks. This relatively brief suckling stage is unusual among arboreal folivores, many of which exhibit more prolonged parental care, but it aligns with the sloth’s need to minimize overall maternal energetic output. The pup’s ability to consume solid food at this early stage is facilitated by the specialized, bacteria-rich gut flora that begins to establish during the nursing period.

Puberty in the brown-throated sloth, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the first potential for reproductive engagement, is reached at approximately 1642 days since birth [tp = approximately 1642 days since birth] at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a value estimated from long-term field studies of the related three-toed sloth Bradypus tridactylus. This exceedingly slow maturation is one of the slowest recorded for any mammal of similar mass, underscoring the species’ extreme adherence to a low-metabolism, low-energetic-output lifestyle. The long juvenile period is spent almost entirely solitary within a small home range, feeding on a monotonous diet of Cecropia leaves, which provides only marginal nutritional returns. This protracted developmental phase allows for the gradual accumulation of body mass and the full development of the sloth’s specialized musculoskeletal adaptations for suspensory locomotion. Reaching sexual maturity marks the beginning of a reproductively viable phase that will occupy the majority of the sloth's remaining lifespan.

The maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 35 years [am = 35 years] at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a remarkably long duration for a mammal of its body size. This exceptional longevity is made possible by a combination of a predator-defended arboreal niche, a low-quality diet that demands minimal foraging movements, and an extraordinarily low intrinsic metabolic rate. At a typical body temperature of 33 °C, the animal’s resting oxygen consumption reaches 686 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 686 milliliters of oxygen per hour]; this constitutes the species’ maximum basal metabolic rate under those conditions at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This value is markedly lower than allometric predictions for a 5-kilogram placental mammal, a discrepancy that has long fascinated comparative physiologists. The reduced metabolic heat production is directly linked to the sloth’s relatively low and variable core body temperature, which fluctuates with ambient conditions to conserve energy.

The species’ maximum reproductive rate is exceptionally low, with females producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and typically raising just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year] at 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This pacing is tightly linked to the energy constraints imposed by a leaf-based diet; under these thermally stable conditions, the energetic costs of gestation and lactation are met only through a slow, sustained draw on maternal reserves. The period from one parturition to the next is thus lengthy, and reproductive output over an entire lifetime is consequently very low. This strategy is characteristic of a "slow" life-history continuum, where each offspring receives an extended period of maternal investment that increases its probability of survival in a challenging, resource-poor environment. Ultimately, the combination of extreme longevity and extremely low annual fecundity defines the brown-throated sloth as one of the most energetically conservative mammals ever studied.
